column9: Megillah 10b: ‘Rabbi Elazar said that this is how the matter is to be understood: Indeed, God Himself does not rejoice over the downfall of the wicked, but He causes others to rejoice. The Gemara comments: One can learn from the language of the verse as well, as it is written: “So the Lord will rejoice [ken yasis]” (Deuteronomy 28:63). And it is not written yasus, the grammatical form of the verb meaning: He will rejoice. Rather, it is written yasis. The grammatical form of this verb indicates that one causes another to rejoice. Consequently, these words are understood to mean that God will cause others to rejoice. The Gemara concludes: Indeed, learn from it that this is the case.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 19 — Holy Anger: Awakening the Heart to Serve Hashem, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 10b) to illuminate his statement here (“only the true meaning of "in laughter" aligns with what we explained regarding what is written (Megillah 10b): "He Himself does not rejoice, but He causes others to rejoice", for even though the Blessed Name does not...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

column13: Whereby he grasped the cause: that Hashem was filled with sovereign favor, having chosen the preservation of the world, swearing: “I will not again curse the ground”; filling all worlds with this resolve, which echoed into the human heart, resolving likewise: I will not again expand lawlessly as before. And though superficially it appears that because of the sweet savor ascending from creation Hashem swore “I will not again”; in truth the reverse is true: because Hashem was filled with sovereign favor, Noah was inspired to offer that sweet savor, as written (Psalms 10:17): “You will direct their heart, You will cause Your ear to hear.”
